long_form.title_primary: The Company That Shipped Bricks and Called Them Hard Drives
title_challengers: The Bricks That Passed a Real Audit
To Hit Their Numbers, They Shipped 26,000 Bricks
long_form.description:
In the late 1980s, MiniScribe was one of the hottest hard-drive makers in America. To hide a hole in its books, it shipped 26,000 hard drives that were actually bricks.

Under a celebrated turnaround CEO who ran the place by fear, MiniScribe's managers faked the one thing auditors are supposed to physically verify: the inventory. They picked the locks on the auditors' own boxes to swap the count, then bought 26,000 real bricks, packed them into hard-drive boxes with fake serial numbers, and shipped the same fakes around the world so they could count them twice. It passed a professional audit. This is how a warehouse of bricks became four million dollars of cutting-edge technology, how the whole thing finally came apart, and why the record-breaking verdict against the auditors was never actually paid.

Sources:
- "MiniScribe," Wikipedia: the backbone, covering the brick scheme and 26,000 count, the ~$4M in-transit booking, the double-count via shipped-and-returned units, the Coopers and Lybrand test-count and lock-box tampering, the layoff-driven exposure, the massive-fraud / run-amok board finding, the bankruptcy and Maxtor sale, the Wiles conviction and the insider-trading share sale, and the Hambrecht and Quist role.
- The Silicon Underground (Dave Farquhar), "Miniscribe Brick: A hard drive scandal": the rented second Colorado warehouse, the weight-matched and shrink-wrapped packing, the scrap and defective drives re-counted as inventory, the pre-agreed customer returns, and the remote-management, quota-pressure culture.
- StorageNewsletter, "History (1989): Unbelievable! Miniscribe Shipped Bricks Rather than HDDs" (2019): the restated losses and negative net worth, the bankruptcy and Maxtor figures, and the roughly $128 million June 1992 settlement.
- businessblunders.com, "Q.T. Wiles, MiniScribe": the Colorado Brick Co. supplier, the Doctor Fix-It reputation, the stand-up-and-fire meeting, and the Allen-wrench and paper-clip lock-picking.
- UPI Archives, "Judge overturns $550 million MiniScribe verdict" (1992) and "Accountants cited in verdict" (1992): the $550 million jury verdict, the $200 million against Coopers and Lybrand and $45 million against Hambrecht and Quist, and the judge's reversal for insufficient evidence.

primary.concept: Pairs with 'The Company That Shipped Bricks and Called Them Hard Drives.' One dominant object: a single plain clay brick sitting inside an open, torn-open hard-drive shipping box, clean 2.5D vector, flat cel shading, on a single-color field with ~60% negative space, no face. The one red accent is a small official price/valuation stamp reading on the brick. Overlay '$4,000,000' is the value the books claimed for the box, set against a literal rock, so title + thumbnail open the loop together (a company that called bricks hard drives, and a four-million-dollar brick) without either restating the other.

challengers.concept: Pairs with 'The Bricks That Passed a Real Audit.' One dominant object: a shrink-wrapped hard-drive box with a green auditor's checkmark / APPROVED stamp on it, and just visible through the plastic, the corner of a clay brick instead of a drive. Clean 2.5D vector, flat cel, single-color field, >=55% negative space, no face. One red accent (a thin red seal edge) hints something is wrong. Overlay 'It passed.' is the forbidden-knowledge gag (a warehouse of bricks cleared a professional audit), a reframe of the how-did-nobody-check payload, not a restatement of the title.

Pairs with 'To Hit Their Numbers, They Shipped 26,000 Bricks.' One dominant subject: a tall pallet stack of identical hard-drive boxes shrink-wrapped together, with a single box cracked open at the corner revealing a clay brick. Clean 2.5D vector, flat cel, single-color field, >=50% negative space, no face. The one red accent is a small red inventory tag on the pallet. Overlay '26,000 bricks' names the scale of the fake stock, pairing with the pressure-culture title (they packed bricks to make a number) rather than restating it.

long_form.pinned_comment: The part that still gets me: the auditors never opened most of the boxes. They spot-checked a sample and trusted the paperwork, and the paperwork had already been rewritten by someone who picked the lock on their box with a paperclip. What gets you more: that senior people at a real tech company packed 26,000 actual bricks by hand, or that the only reason it ever came out is they laid off the exact people who did the packing?
